newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac drops deadline for French NATO decision.
newsitem.headline: Chirac drops deadline for French NATO decision.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac has quietly dropped a self-imposed May deadline for deciding whether France should return to NATO's military command after a 30-year absence, French officials say.
Negotiations with the United States are continuing and the timing of France's campaign for a snap May 25-June 1 parliamentary election was also a reason to delay a decision, they said.

Chirac told U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright in January that he would take his decision in May, well before a planned July summit in Madrid to decide on the reform and enlargement of the 16-nation defence alliance.

The official reason for postponing the strategic choice is that Paris and Washington are still talking at diplomatic and military levels on the disputed issue of the future of the alliance's southern command, which controls the Mediterranean.
France says the Americans must hand over the Naples-based command - which they have long held - to a European, or at least share responsibility equally.

The Clinton administration has refused, citing the vital importance of the U.S. Sixth Fleet, its Middle East role and value as a broker between feuding NATO allies Greece and Turkey. It is offering the Europeans a bigger subordinate role.

"There is no longer really a deadline. The technical negotiations are not yet concluded. We want to detach this Franco-American problem from the success of the Madrid summit," a French official familiar with the talks said.
"There will be a success in Madrid anyway, with a structural reform establishing a European pillar of NATO. The question of France's place is disconnected," he said.
Insiders acknowledge that Chirac wanted to avoid taking a decision in the middle of the parliamentary election campaign.
The Socialist and Communist opposition have accused him of selling out to the Americans by moving back towards NATO without winning anything in exchange.

Some old guard Gaullists in Chirac's own RPR party also oppose integrating France fully into a U.S.-dominated military command from which his political mentor, president Charles de Gaulle, withdrew French forces in 1966.

"If Chirac had to decide before the election, he would probably have to say 'no', since the Americans won't hand over southern command. After the vote, if the right is re-elected, his hands will be free," a European diplomat said.
That does not necessarily mean France will definitely return in July to NATO's integrated military structure.
French officials insist the decision depends on gaining "visible shared responsibility" at AFSOUTH, as the Naples headquarters is known in NATO jargon.

Diplomats say Washington is seeking a compromise around the idea of a European deputy southern commander with specific duties for European operations, with a sweetener for the French in commanding a Mediterranean rapid reaction force.

Delaying the French decision also removed a potential stumbling block to holding a May 27 NATO-Russia summit in Paris to sign an agreement laying the foundations of post-Cold War European security arrangements.
Chirac was keen to host the prestige gathering between the two rounds of the election to show voters that France was playing a major role in the new NATO, diplomats said.
